The Commission records that Moldova signed a cooperation agreement with the European Labour Authority in May 2025, which covers the arrangements for cooperating with it. The government states that the draft law to harmonise national legislation with Regulation (EU) 2019/1149 is still being prepared, and gives this only as its own account. What remains is adopting and applying the law that aligns national legislation with the regulation, including the Authority's role as mediator, and building the capacity of the ministry, the employment agency and the labour inspectorate to cooperate with it.

No item among the 7 Moldova items on this issue is a Commission requirement, key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition; the Commission mentions the issue only to record the 2025 cooperation agreement. Cooperation with the Authority is a small part of the chapter.

The change is narrow, legal and within the control of the labour ministry, and the cooperation agreement was concluded in 2025, which shows recent progress with the Authority. A draft law has already been identified, although its adoption date is not given.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is only part of the chapter and no sub-area wording matches. The 2023 report, the 2023 Analytical Report and the 2024 report all find that EU rules on supplementary pension rights of mobile workers are not incorporated into Moldovan law and that there is no occupational pension scheme, and in 2025 the government still describes the occupational system as at an early stage and plans full transposition of Directive 98/49/EC.

Sources conflict: the Commission in 2024 says the EU rules are not incorporated into Moldovan law, while the government in 2025 says, on the basis of the financial market regulator's conformity tables, that the law is aligned with Directive 2014/50/EU and partly transposes Directive 98/49/EC. The responses named by the government, full transposition of Directive 98/49/EC and a draft amendment to Law No. 198/2020, are not yet adopted. What remains is incorporating the EU rules on acquiring and preserving supplementary pension rights into Moldovan law in a form the Commission accepts.

The finding is repeated in the 2023 and 2024 reports but is not named in a key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition among the 11 Moldova items on this issue. Moldova has no occupational pension scheme, so the rules have limited practical reach, and the issue is a small part of the chapter.

The change is legal and lies with the government and the financial market regulator, and a draft amendment to the voluntary pension funds law is identified. Against that, the government and the Commission disagree on how far the law is already aligned, and no adoption date is given for the draft.

The chapter scale was used as context only, since this is part of the chapter; the issue's own items show change. The 2023 report and Analytical Report and the 2024 report find that no authority is responsible for open data policies, and the 2025 report finds Moldova not yet aligned with the Open Data Directive; the 2026 report records a law partially harmonising with that Directive, and the government reports a dedicated open data unit created in the economy ministry under Law No. 109/2025. The improvement is legal and institutional only, since no item measures publication or re-use of data.

The law on open data and re-use, its methodological rules and a two-person policy unit address the Commission's findings on alignment and on the absence of a responsible authority, but the law only partly transposes the Directive. The government itself says the data.gov.md portal needs updating and completing with data, the World Bank finds the portal still lacking in use, and the draft law on data governance has been suspended until 2027. What remains is full alignment with the Open Data Directive and related EU data rules, and regular publication and updating of datasets by institutions on the portal.

The Commission repeats the finding on open data in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and the 2024 Growth Plan Communication refers to implementing the Open Data Directive, but no item among the 87 Moldova items on this issue is a key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition. Open data is a defined part of the data theme rather than its centre.

Recent legal progress is recorded, with a law, methodological rules and a responsible unit in place, and the portal already exists. Against that, capacity is thin, with two posts in the ministry and one at the e-Governance Agency for the portal, and publication depends on many institutions, including local authorities, whose capacity the government lists as a challenge.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is only part of the chapter. The 2023 report finds 39 staff for 45 posts with high turnover, the 2024 and 2025 reports call for more capacity, especially staff, and the 2026 report says the authority's human, technical and financial capacities have not grown with its expanded mandate. The authority's own 2025 report gives 36 staff at the end of 2025 and a turnover rate of 18%, which confirms the finding but is its own account.

The Commission's latest finding is that capacities remain limited while Law No. 195/2024 has widened the mandate, and the only response directly aimed at capacity, strengthening the authority's administrative and human resources, has not yet been carried out. The authority itself reports pay below comparable supervisory bodies, staff overload and pressure on staff, and gives this as its own account. What remains is giving the National Centre for Personal Data Protection the staff, pay, budget and safeguards it needs to supervise independently under the new law.

An adequately resourced and independent supervisory authority is a core requirement of the EU data protection acquis, and the Commission records the shortfall in the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports with no increase in capacity recorded, which meets the test for High without a benchmark. The 2025 Enlargement Communication's call for more resources and independence for data protection authorities applies to all enlargement countries and only supports this.

The remedy is within the government's control, through the staffing limit, pay and budget, and Law No. 195/2024 was adopted. Against that, staff numbers fell from 39 in 2022 to 36 at the end of 2025 despite repeated recommendations, and the authority links turnover to pay below comparable bodies, which needs wider pay decisions.

The chapter scale was used as context only, since this is part of the chapter. The 2023 report asks Moldova to join the third-country trusted list and the 2024 report asks for interoperability with European Digital Identity Wallets; the 2026 report records amendments in December 2025 that fully align the rules for qualified trust service providers, joining the trusted list and cross-border testing of the national wallet. Use has not changed in the same way: the Commission gives 200 000 users, 9.8% of adults, in 2024 and over 266 000, 10% of adults, in 2025.

Recognition has advanced through the December 2025 amendments, the trusted list and new identity cards carrying a qualified signature, but the Reform Agenda condition for December 2026 also requires an EU-aligned national wallet integrating at least 20 e-services, and the wallet was only started in September 2025, with remote identification moved to 2027. Use remains low, with about 10% of the population holding qualified certificates and fees of at least 11 euros a year reported by civil society in 2026. What remains is a working EU-aligned wallet, mutual recognition in practice and much wider, cheaper use of electronic identification and signatures.

The national wallet aligned with EU standards, joining the third-country trusted list and alignment with eIDAS 2 are a Reform Agenda payment condition due in December 2026, and the Commission raised the trusted list and wallet interoperability in the 2023 and 2024 reports. Electronic identification is the centre of this theme.

Legal and recognition steps have moved quickly, with Law No. 117/2025, the December 2025 amendments and the trusted list, and the work lies mainly with the e-Governance Agency and the trust service provider. Against that, use has stayed near 10% of adults, the eKYC deadline has slipped to 2027, and within the 2025 consultation another government body described EVOSign as still at the pilot stage and not ready for use in systems.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since the issue comes from a cross-cutting theme. In 2023 the Commission finds no electronic biometric database and asks for planning towards Eurodac, and in 2026 it finds security and data protection weaknesses in the border police system and asks for interoperability ahead of a future connection to EU large-scale systems; no item among the 27 Moldova items on this issue comes from the 2024 or 2025 reports. Wider use of SIENA, which the 2026 report records, is the one change, and it concerns Europol's exchange channel rather than the EU systems in this issue.

Apart from SIENA, the responses to the latest requirements are plans: interoperability of the fingerprint register with Eurodac, a national visa system interoperable with VIS, interoperability of the criminal records register with ECRIS and ECRIS-TCN by 2027, and a joint study with eu-LISA. The government reports a partial transposition of the Eurodac regulation in the fingerprint law, which is legal only. What remains is building or upgrading the migration, border and justice systems so that they are secure and ready to connect to Eurodac, VIS, ECRIS and the other EU large-scale systems.

The Commission repeats the call for data exchange through SIENA in the 2023 and 2026 key recommendations and raises Eurodac and EU large-scale systems in 2023 and 2026, but connection to most of these systems is expected only towards accession and no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition was found among the 27 Moldova items on this issue.

There is evidence of progress on SIENA, rolled out to several law enforcement bodies, and the government has a plan covering each system. Against that, the work needs the interior ministry, the migration inspectorate, the border police, justice bodies and eu-LISA, and the systems for Eurodac and VIS are still to be built or upgraded.

The chapter scales were not decisive, since this issue spans several chapters and is part of each. The main thread is taxation: the Commission finds no IT strategy for interoperability with EU tax systems in 2023 and 2024, records a programme prepared in 2025, and in 2026 records a roadmap for 2026 to 2029 while finding that EMCS and SEED solutions remain to be developed and that VIES interoperability must advance. The plans are adopted but no new connection to an EU system is recorded, and the 2026 report adds that Moldova is not yet in ECURIE or EURDEP.

Some connections exist, such as access to TED since 2020, trademark data in EUIPO systems and use of TRACES, but they lie outside the latest requirements. The responses to those requirements are a tax IT programme and roadmap that are adopted, and connections to the CCN gateway, VIES and other tax systems, TESTA and IMI that are planned. What remains is building and connecting the tax, excise, radiological, civil protection and internal market systems to the EU systems the Commission names.

Tax interoperability is a core acquis requirement raised in the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, but the Commission records good progress in the taxation chapter in 2025 and 2026, so the test for High on lack of progress is not met, and no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition was found among the 56 Moldova items on this issue. The issue groups many sectors, each with one or two items.

The tax service now has an approved IT programme and a roadmap with a timetable, which is evidence of planning progress. Against that, the work spreads across many agencies and EU systems, and some connections depend on EU arrangements open only to Member States, as the government notes for the AGORA system.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since the issue comes from a cross-cutting theme and its items sit in the economic sections. The Commission finds that digitalisation is lagging behind in 2023, slowly improving in 2024, steadily advancing in 2025 and continuing to advance in 2026. These findings concern the economy as a whole; no item among the 71 Moldova items on this issue gives a change over time in business adoption itself.

Responses are in place: SME digitalisation programmes, association to the Digital Europe Programme and the first European Digital Innovation Hub, launched in April 2026. Against that, the Reform Agenda finds the share of businesses using digital services low, and the government's 2025 programme still gives a baseline of 0.9% of enterprises making web sales. What remains is wider adoption of digital technologies by small businesses and greater use of EU programmes and the new innovation hub.

The Commission's findings on this issue are general statements in the economic sections, positive since 2024, and no item among the 71 Moldova items on this issue is a key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on business adoption. Business adoption is not an acquis requirement.

Support programmes, EU funding routes and the first innovation hub exist, and the Commission records steady progress in digitalisation. Against that, adoption depends on many small firms, and the government cites lack of knowledge, high costs and perceived long-term returns as barriers.

The chapter scale was used as context only, since this is part of the chapter. The Commission finds about 40% of mapped services available digitally in 2024, over 50% in 2025 with 64% for businesses and 54% for individuals in 2024, and 82% of business services and 61% of citizen services by June 2026, and its 2026 release decision confirms that the Reform Agenda objective of 75% of business services was met. The 2026 report also finds that user uptake increased significantly, including in rural areas.

The business services reform is in place, with the State Register of Legal Units launched in December 2025 and the life events methodology approved, and the Commission judges the payment step satisfactorily fulfilled. Still, only 133 of the 414 business services counted are fully digital end to end, citizen services lag at 61%, the Commission noted low demand in 2025, and the systems of the entrepreneurship agency and the employment agency are still being procured or built. What remains is end-to-end online delivery and wider use of sector services, especially for citizens and in agencies such as the entrepreneurship and employment agencies.

Digital services for businesses are a Reform Agenda payment condition, and the Commission's key recommendations call for digitalising processes to cut administrative burden in 2023 and 2024 and for digitalising the entrepreneurship agency's processes in 2025 and 2026. Online public services are central to the digital government theme.

There is strong evidence of past progress, with the share of business services online rising each year from 2024 to 2026 and the payment step met. The work is led by the e-Governance Agency and the State Chancellery with shared platforms, although sector agencies and rural demand still need attention.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since the issue comes from a cross-cutting theme. The Commission finds the e-procurement system inadequate in 2021, calls for it to be overhauled or re-engineered in 2023, describes MTender as outdated in 2025, and in 2026 records limited progress on digitalising procurement and an outdated MTender that limits monitoring; no item among the 44 Moldova items on this issue comes from the 2024 report.

The new system is still being procured: technical specifications were received in September 2025 and the call for bids was published in December 2025 with a deadline in February 2026, while the Reform Agenda sets a pilot of the new system by December 2027. MTender remains in use without planning, contract management and some procedures. What remains is designing, building and putting into operation a new e-procurement system that covers every procedure and stage of the procurement cycle.

The new e-procurement system is a Reform Agenda payment condition, recalled in the 2025 release decision, and the Commission calls for it in the 2023 report and in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports. It is central to digital public procurement.

Funding from international partners is secured, a concept and programme exist, and procurement of the system has started with World Bank review. Against that, the system has been called for since 2021 with limited progress recorded in 2026, and building a full new system is a large technical project.
